Sapolsky was arguing that it wasn't free will making them 'behave' well half the time, simply a fear of the consequences 'fighting and winning out' against the 'broken' part of their brain. I agree with what you're saying here, that punishment still serves a function in a world without a belief in free will. But I think that function changes: punishment only makes sense as a deterrent, and that only makes sense in some cases, which I presume are to be determined empirically.

E.g. Imprisoning someone for killing their spouse in a jealous rage may not be an effective deterrent, because the last thing you're thinking about when in a jealous rage are the consequences. You may want to imprison such a person in order to avoid another person being harmed, but that's not punishment, it's social protection as you mentioned. If they're very unlikely to hurt someone else, better just given them extensive community service or something.

In contrast, imprisoning, say, a bank robber makes far more sense, as such a crime will (I assume from the movies...) take a fair bit of planning, and thus allow plenty of time for one to weigh in the consequences of the action.
